analysis.one_liner: Caps fees private debt collectors can charge on federal debts and applies consumer protections to government debt collection.
analysis.headline: The bill never received committee action and died in the Senate Banking Committee without a vote, despite a bipartisan sponsor-cosponsor pair.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the main federal debt-collection law, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, to debts people owe to federal agencies like fines, penalties, and overpayments. It bars a federal agency from selling a debt to a private collector within 90 days and requires three advance notices before doing so. It also limits what a collector collecting for a federal agency can add on: any fee must be reasonable, allowed by contract, and no more than 10% of the amount collected. Finally, it directs a government watchdog study of how governments at all levels use private debt collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: People who owe money to a federal agency — a fine, penalty, fee, or overpayment at least 180 days past due — who today can be pursued by private collectors adding fees, fees that face few of the normal consumer protections. Under the bill, collectors could not pile on charges that are unreasonable, uncontracted, or above 10% of the amount collected, and consumers would get at least three notices, spaced a month apart, before their debt is handed to a private collector.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People owing fines and fees to federal agencies

how_it_helps.text: Defines debt under the law to include obligations to a federal agency — a loan, overpayment, fine, penalty, or fee — at least 180 days past due, so collectors of federal debts come under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act's abuse and harassment prohibitions [S2][S3].

Bars a federal agency from selling or transferring such a debt to a collector until at least 90 days after the obligation arises, and requires the agency to notify the consumer at least three times, with at least 30 days between the later notices, before handing the debt over [S2][S3].

Stops collectors collecting for federal agencies from adding any interest, fee, charge, or expense that is unreasonable relative to actual costs, not authorized by their government contract, or greater than 10% of the amount collected [S2][S3].

Requires the Government Accountability Office to study and report within a year on how federal, state, and local governments use private debt collectors, including their contract selection, the extra fees charged to debtors, revenue-sharing deals, court-judgment tactics, and any legal immunity collectors enjoy [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private debt collection firms and debt buyers, which would lose a large, lightly regulated market: collecting government fines and fees with add-on charges and little oversight. Federal agencies would also have to hold debts 90 days and send notices before transferring them, adding administrative work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private debt collectors and debt buyers

drawbacks.text: The protections reach only debts at least 180 days past due and owed to federal agencies, leaving out more recent and non-federal debts, so the help is narrower than the bill's title suggests [S3].

Tight limits on fees and on when debts can be handed over could make private collectors less willing to take on hard-to-collect government debts, pushing agencies to rely on their own tools like garnishment instead, which shifts collection practices rather than reducing them [S3].
The GAO study and report add reporting work but change nothing by themselves; the bill's substantive effect depends entirely on the fee cap and notice rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who owe federal debts, the benefits are real: fewer surprise fees, a 10% cap on add-on charges, and advance notice before a private collector gets their debt. The costs fall almost entirely on the debt collection industry, which is the point. The main honest criticism is that the bill is narrower than its title — it covers only federal debts already 180 days past due — and much of it is a study rather than new rules. It is a modest, targeted consumer protection bill, not a broad overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took any action on it before the Congress ended, so it never got a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Cory Booker introduced the bill on September 19, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no Senate vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill carried bipartisan sponsorship, with Senator Mike Lee listed as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private debt collection firms that contract with government agencies are better off: they kept collecting federal fines, fees, and overpayments free of the fee caps, notice requirements, and consumer protections this bill would have imposed, and the promised federal study of that arrangement never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors that hold government contracts

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors; it was referred to the Banking Committee

against.name: Sherrod Brown and members of the Senate Banking Committee
against.what_they_did: No member moved the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, did not schedule any markup or consideration of the bill during the two-plus years after referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — a Democrat and a conservative Republican — but because it never reached a committee or floor vote, no one ever had to take a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Debt collection agencies and debt buyers
industries.note: The bill caps at 10% the fees collectors can charge on debts owed to federal agencies, requires a contract and a reasonableness test for any charge, and subjects federal-debt collection to the main federal consumer debt law. That directly reduces revenue and flexibility in a business built on collecting government fines, fees, and overpayments with add-on charges.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local government agencies that hire private collectors
industries.note: Federal agencies would face a 90-day holding period and a three-notice requirement before transferring debts, which costs administrative effort but could shield them from public criticism of aggressive outsourced collection. The bill's GAO study would also expose state and local contracting practices and revenue-sharing deals.
